title: La Traviata
facts: La Traviata premiered on 6 March 1853 at La Fenice in Venice.
The day after the premiere, Verdi wrote his most famous letter: “La traviata last night a failure. Was the fault mine or the singers’? Time will tell.”
Verdi, letter to Emanuele Muzio, 1853 (via Wikipedia)
The premiere audience jeered at times, some of it aimed at the casting of Fanny Salvini-Donatelli as Violetta.
Revised and revived in 1854, it was a hit. Piave reported: “Then it was a fiasco; now it has created a furore. Draw your own conclusions!”
Verdi wanted a contemporary setting, but La Fenice insisted on the past (“c. 1700”). Realistic modern-dress productions came only in the 1880s.
The story comes from La Dame aux camélias by Alexandre Dumas fils, which Verdi saw in Paris with Giuseppina Strepponi in 1852.
By coincidence, an Italian translation of the Dumas play was running just down the street from La Fenice at the premiere.
Verdi told Piave he wanted something new: “I don’t want any of those everyday subjects that one can find by the hundreds.”
Verdi arrived in Venice for rehearsals “filled with premonitions of disaster” and made his unhappiness clear to the singers.
The prelude opens with very soft, very high strings portraying the frail heroine, then the main love theme on lower strings.
Asked for a toast, Alfredo sings the brindisi “Libiamo ne’ lieti calici”, “Let’s drink from the joyful cups”.
After the Brindisi, an offstage band plays waltzes. Waltz rhythms run through Act I to create a Parisian atmosphere.
The long Germont–Violetta duet is built in many sections, the music following each turn of the drama.
“Di Provenza il mar, il suol”: Germont tries to comfort his son by reminding him of home in Provence.
At Flora’s party, guests dress up as gypsy girls and matadors from Madrid to entertain.
In New York, diarist George Templeton Strong shrugged at the scandal: the plot was no worse than Don Giovanni, which on stage was “little but rampant lechery”.
La Traviata is among the most frequently performed of all operas.
